html:
During Prohibition in the United States, from 1920 to 1933, the Bahamas became a main base for smuggling liquor into Florida. Nassau and the island of Bimini, only about 80 kilometres from Miami, boomed.

British law allowed the liquor trade, so merchants imported whisky and rum legally and sold it to fast boats that ran it across to the American coast. The government grew rich on import duties.

The trade echoed an earlier boom, when Nassau served Confederate blockade runners in the American Civil War. When Prohibition ended the islands slumped, until tourism took off after World War II and later under Lynden Pindling.
